newsitem.title: USA: Columbia/HCA-Tenet merger talk viewed skeptically.
newsitem.headline: Columbia/HCA-Tenet merger talk viewed skeptically.

text.p: Talk of a possible merger between the embattled Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp and the much smaller Tenet Healthcare Corp struck most Wall Street analysts on Wednesday as far-fetched.
None was willing to rule out such a deal, however, given the surplus of surprises recently surrounding Columbia/HCA, the largest U.S. for-profit hospital company.
"I'm sort of surprised by the timing here, but I imagine it's a doable deal," said Helen O'Donnell, healthcare industry analyst at PaineWebber.

"It could make sense in terms of both companies extending their geographic focus. But I'm a little surprised that Columbia is interested, if in fact they are interested, at such price levels," O'Donnell said.
Tenet's facilities are concentrated in California, with major operations also in Texas and Florida. Columbia/HCA's biggest markets are in Tennessee, Kentucky, Georgia, Florida and Texas.
The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Columbia/HCA and Tenet are holding discussions about a possible combination, according to unnamed sources.
Spokespersons for both companies, contacted Wednesday, refused to comment on the report.

Columbia/HCA, based in Nashville, Tenn., had 1996 revenues of $19.9 billion. It runs 342 hospitals, 150 surgery centers and more than 570 home health locations in 36 states, England, Switzerland and Spain.

Tenet, based in Santa Barbara, Calif., operates 130 hospitals in 22 states and reported revenues of $5.5 billion in fiscal 1996 ended last May. In January, Tenet acquired OrNda HealthCorp for about $1.8 billion. The combined companies would have annual revenues of about $8.5 billion.
Shares in both companies rallied Wednesday on the New York Stock Exchange in heavy trading volume. Columbia/HCA closed up 3-1/4 at 36-3/8; Tenet was up 2-5/8 at 30-1/8.

Short covering may have been behind much of the rally in Columbia/HCA, which was hit last week by a massive government investigation that involved raids by hundreds of federal agents on company facilities in six states, analysts said.
Confusion over which company would be the likely survivor of a merger might also have partially explained the unusual rally of both stocks, analysts said.
In comments on a possible merger, some analysts saw Columbia/HCA as the buyer and others saw Tenet in that role.
"Frankly, I think it's kind of a smoke-screen. To me, it makes absolutely no sense at all," said Robert Gold, healthcare industry analyst at S&P Equity Group.

"Tenet is in the process of assimilating OrNda and Columbia is acquiring Value Health. That's aside from all the federal investigation problems ... If a merger like that was announced, if it ever actually went through, to me it would be a negative development because it would be another operational problem for Columbia to overcome," Gold said.
Other analysts built a scenario, however, in which Tenet could acquire Columbia/HCA.
"We believe an offer by Tenet to buy Columbia is not as far-fetched as it might first appear," said Bear Stearns healthcare industry analyst Albert Rice.

"Tenet trades at nearly a four price/earnings multiple-point premium to Columbia/HCA. Both companies are capable of completing a pooling of interest acquisition currently," Rice said, "Tenet's CEO has a history of being able to obtain positive results in government negotiations ... A Tenet/Columbia transaction would be compelling economically."
